title: Hiring Jack Scott and Teddy Edwards from Mississippi
summary: Fields signs guitarist Jack Scott and his friend Teddy Edwards, whom he puts in charge of the reed section.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Well, before you go talking about that, I want to mention one more man before we got onto "In The Mood".

You spoke about him before, Teddy Edwards. Teddy Edwards--I had a habit--I don't have a lot, you know you can't take it with you, but I think I would have been more successful with money if I could just pass up a good musician, but when I saw a good one I couldn't pass it up. Do you know King Kolax?
Well Kolax was in a band once but some people say that was a habit King Kolax had--he would have maybe twelve or fifteen people and didn't need them, but if they were good that was it.

So this thing about Teddy Edwards, I was looking for a guitar player and somebody had gone down south and inquired because as you say, (inaudible), and I was told about Jack Scott--Ernest Scott is his real name but he's known as Jack Scott--a guitar player, arranger,

and also he played piano, and so I talked with Jack and he was for it. I think it was in Jackson, Mississippi but they were originally out of Laurel, Mississippi and talked around, so you know how some of these guys are, I don't like to get into it, but like that buddy, you got to hire one with the other, but at the same time, I went to this little gig that they were playing, and I tell you the truth, I was just carried away with Teddy Edwards and so, they didn't have to influence me much about getting Teddy when Jack said now I'll go but Teddy wants to join you too.

I kind of played hard to get but I was glad to say yeah and I sent back later and got Jack and Teddy Edwards, and Teddy Edwards turned out just very sensational. I turned the reed section over to him and he worked with the guys. He was a nice musician; he could work with the brass men, but he meant a lot to my reed section.
I think I was the one that sug-
What was he playing with you?

He was playing alto, and then he picked up tenor a little there and I told him, I said Teddy, 'I believe you ought to stick with it. Did you know we lost Teddy a couple of years ago, he was very, very ill.
Yes, I know. I did a lot of work with him.
That's when he left the band, I can't blame him, you know, the travelling and he saw he could make it in one place.
